reasoning_traces.think:
Formal means-end capacity (FMEC) is foundational, encoding an organism’s ability to anticipate and navigate relational structures without explicit dimensional context. It is defined by a set of formal relations including direction, distance, sequence, similarity, reversibility, closure, hierarchy, and alternativeness. These relations form a topological lattice underpinning anticipatory behavior. Dimensional means-end capacity (DMEC) extends FMEC by embedding these formal relations into specific media—such as space, time, language, or physiology—thereby enabling concrete action. DMEC is mathematically modeled as a fiber bundle over a base space of dimensional media, where fibers encode formal relations. Manipulanda capacity (MC) provides the operational grounding: it allows organisms to act upon and perceive the immediate means-objects that instantiate formal relations. Together, these primitives define a triadic cognitive architecture: FMEC supplies structure, DMEC supplies context, and MC supplies execution. Failure modes include: inability to form formal relations (FMEC breakdown), inability to map to dimensional media (DMEC breakdown), or inability to manipulate objects (MC breakdown). Each mode introduces distinct epistemic uncertainty in prediction and control.
